title: Portfolio site + README craft
summary: Build a clean portfolio site and write READMEs that make recruiters understand and trust your projects in seconds.
objectives: Understand what a hiring manager actually looks for in a portfolio
Structure a README that explains what, why, and how
Add setup, usage, and demo sections people can follow
Publish a simple portfolio site with GitHub Pages
Pin and order your best repositories on GitHub
Write project descriptions that lead with impact, not tech
Avoid the common mistakes that get portfolios ignored

quiz.q: What is the single most important section a README should open with?
options: A one-line description of what the project does
A list of every dependency version
quiz.why: A reader decides in seconds whether to keep reading. A clear one-liner answering 'what is this?' earns that time.

quiz.q: Which file name does GitHub automatically render on a repository's front page?
quiz.why: GitHub looks for README.md (Markdown) in the repo root and renders it as the landing page.

quiz.q: GitHub Pages can host a static site directly from which of these?
options: A branch or /docs folder in your repo
quiz.why: GitHub Pages serves static files from a chosen branch or the /docs folder — no server needed, and it is free.

quiz.q: Why should a project description lead with impact rather than the tech stack?
quiz.answer: Because recruiters and managers care first about what the project does and the problem it solves; the tech stack matters but is secondary.
quiz.why: Impact tells them why the work matters; the stack is easy to skim later. Leading with 'built a churn predictor that flags at-risk users' beats 'used pandas and scikit-learn'.

quiz.q: What does pinning a repository on your GitHub profile do?
quiz.answer: It places that repository at the top of your profile so visitors see your best work first instead of your most recent commit.
quiz.why: You can pin up to six repos. Use them to curate, since visitors rarely scroll past the top of your profile.

quiz.q: Name two things a good 'Usage' section in a README should include.
quiz.answer: A copy-pasteable command to run the project and an example of the expected input and output.
quiz.why: People want to try it fast. A runnable command plus a sample result removes guesswork and proves the project works.

body_markdown:
## Why a portfolio matters Your CV says you can do the work. Your **portfolio proves it**. For someone moving from a maths degree and an L1 support role into A I, a portfolio is the bridge — it turns 'I studied this' into 'here is something I built that runs'. A hiring manager spends seconds, not minutes, on each candidate. Your job is to make those seconds count: clear projects, clear writing, no friction. ## What goes in the portfolio Quality beats quantity. Three or four **finished, well-documented** projects beat twenty half-built ones. For each project show the problem, your approach, the result, and how to run it. Curate ruthlessly. Pin your best work on GitHub so visitors see it first. Delete or archive the noise. ## Anatomy of a great README The README is the front door of every project. Open with a one-line description, then expand. A reliable structure: ```markdown # Project Title One sentence: what it does and who it helps. ## Features - Bullet the key things it does ## Setup ```bash pip install -r requirements.txt ``` ## Usage ```bash python main.py --input data.csv ``` ## Results A chart, a metric, or a short demo. ``` Lead with **impact**, not tech. 'Predicts customer churn with 87% accuracy' beats 'uses scikit-learn'. ## Publishing with GitHub Pages GitHub Pages hosts a static site for free, straight from your repo. Put an `index.html` in a `/docs` folder (or a `gh-pages` branch), enable Pages in repo settings, and you have a live U R L. ```bash mkdir docs echo '

Dami — A I Portfolio

' > docs/index.html git add docs/index.html git commit -m "Add portfolio landing page" git push ``` Then go to Settings, Pages, choose the branch and `/docs` folder, and save. ## Make it easy to read Use headings, short paragraphs, and code blocks people can copy. Add badges for build status or license. Include a screenshot or a GIF — a picture of your project running is worth a thousand words. ## Your task Pick your strongest project, rewrite its README with the structure above, pin it on GitHub, and publish a one-page portfolio with GitHub Pages.

For each project, show the problem you tackled, your approach, the result, and exactly how to run it. Be ruthless about what you show. Curate like an artist choosing pieces for a gallery.

slides.title: The README is the front door
bullets: GitHub renders README.md on the repo page.
Open with one line: what it does, who it helps.
Then expand into features, setup, usage.
If they can't understand it fast, they leave.
slides.narration: Every project has a front door, and that door is the README. GitHub automatically renders the file named README dot M D on your repository's landing page. So open with a single line saying what the project does and who it helps. Then expand. If a visitor can't grasp it quickly, they simply move on.

slides.title: A reliable README structure
bullets: Title plus one-sentence description.
Features, Setup, Usage, Results.
Make every command copy-pasteable.
slides.code:
# Churn Predictor

Flags at-risk users from usage data.

## Setup
pip install -r requirements.txt

## Usage
python main.py --input data.csv
slides.narration: Here's a structure that works for almost any project. A title, then one sentence describing it. Then sections for features, setup, usage, and results. The golden rule: make every command copy-pasteable, so a reader can run your project without thinking. Notice the setup and usage commands here are ready to paste straight into a terminal.

slides.title: Lead with impact
bullets: Say what it does before how it's built.
'87% accuracy' beats 'uses scikit-learn'.
Tech stack matters, but comes second.
Speak to the problem, not the tools.
slides.narration: This is the mistake almost everyone makes. They lead with the tech stack: built with pandas, scikit-learn, and so on. But recruiters care first about what the project does. Predicts customer churn with eighty-seven percent accuracy is far stronger than lists the libraries I used. Lead with impact. The tools can come later.

slides.title: Publish with GitHub Pages
bullets: Free static hosting straight from your repo.
Put index.html in a /docs folder.
Enable Pages in repo settings.
You get a live U R L to share.
slides.code:
mkdir docs echo '

Dami Portfolio

' > docs/index.html git add docs/index.html git commit -m "Add landing page" git push
slides.narration: Now let's get a real site online for free. GitHub Pages hosts static files straight from your repository. Create a docs folder, drop an index dot H T M L file inside, then enable Pages in your repository settings and point it at the docs folder. Within a minute you have a live U R L you can put on your CV and share with anyone.

slides.title: Add an A I demo
bullets: Show a small project actually running.
Keep API keys in environment variables.
A working demo builds instant trust.
slides.code:
from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "Summarise this repo."}])
print(msg.content[0].text)
slides.narration: If one of your projects uses A I, show it running. Here's a tiny example using the Anthropic Claude Messages A P I to summarise a repository. Notice we never hard-code the key. Claude reads it from the ANTHROPIC underscore A P I underscore KEY environment variable. A short, working demo builds more trust than any paragraph of description.

slides.title: Make it easy to read
bullets: Headings, short paragraphs, code blocks.
Add badges for build and license.
Include a screenshot or a short GIF.
A picture of it running is worth a thousand words.
slides.narration: Polish matters. Use clear headings, keep paragraphs short, and give people code blocks they can copy. Add a few badges for things like build status or license. And above all, include a screenshot or a short animated GIF of your project running. A picture of working software is worth a thousand words of prose.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: No README, or a one-line stub.
Leading with tech instead of impact.
Broken setup steps nobody tested.
Twenty unfinished repos, none pinned.
slides.narration: Let's flag the mistakes that get portfolios ignored. One: no README, or a single empty line. Two: leading with the tech stack instead of the impact. Three: setup instructions that don't actually work because you never tested them on a clean machine. And four: a pile of half-finished repos with nothing pinned. Avoid these and you're ahead of most applicants.
